medical.title: Fluctuations in blood pressure over time linked to death and strokes, analysis of UK data finds
medical.summary: Greater variation in blood pressure between research visits was associated with a higher risk of death in a study of more than 57,000 UK Biobank participants. Variation in some blood pressure measures was also associated with stroke. The findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2.

medical.title: Regulator-mandated study finds no link between semaglutide use and pancreatic cancer
medical.summary: New research presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2, found no link between semaglutide use and pancreatic cancer in nationwide registry data from Denmark, Sweden and Norway. The regulator-mandated post-authorization study was presented by Anton Pottegård, a professor at the University of Southern Denmark in Odense, and colleagues.

medical.title: Just 20 seconds of speech could help detect type 2 diabetes using AI-based tool
medical.summary: Signs of type 2 diabetes can be detected in just a few seconds from the way someone talks, according to research being presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2.

medical.title: How moving neighborhood can alter risk of type 2 diabetes
medical.summary: Where someone lives strongly influences their risk of developing type 2 diabetes, new research from Canada suggests. The research was presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2.

medical.title: Supervised physical therapy improves short-term knee pain and function after ACL surgery in young adults
medical.summary: A randomized clinical trial found that supervised physical therapy after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) surgery yielded greater improvements in pain, function and muscle strength than a self-directed exercise program, at least in the short term. The findings can inform care for people with ongoing knee symptoms after ACL surgery. The study is published in Annals of Internal Medicine.

medical.title: Study revisits measures of breastfeeding success—and the consequences for parents
medical.summary: Within breastfeeding research, there's a widely recognized need to move beyond using only the duration of breastfeeding as the measure of "successful breastfeeding" and to integrate person-centered outcomes.

medical.title: Bedside blood test can deliver results in under 10 minutes to guide urgent stroke care
medical.summary: Minutes count when a patient with a stroke arrives at a hospital emergency room. Doctors stand ready to treat the patient, but whether medication can dissolve the blood clot depends on what the patient is already taking. Even if a blood sample is rushed to the laboratory, results can take up to an hour to arrive.

medical.title: Lower dietary diversity in the first year linked to atopic dermatitis
medical.summary: Lower dietary diversity during the first year of life is associated with an increased risk of atopic dermatitis (AD) later in life, according to a study published online Sept. 20 in Pediatric Allergy and Immunology.

medical.title: Metabolic activity of gut bacteria can either promote or inhibit function of CAR T cells in cancer therapy
medical.summary: Immunotherapies, especially CAR T-cell therapy, have fundamentally changed cancer treatment in recent years, particularly for certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma. Yet not all tumors respond equally well, and the reasons for this remain incompletely understood. A new multicenter study by the Leibniz Institute for Immunotherapy collaboration group, Innate Immune Sensing in Cancer and Transplantation, now shows that it is not only the composition of the gut microbiota that determines the success of CAR T-cell therapy, but above all its metabolic products.

medical.title: Abuse and disability trap: 90% of incarcerated Michigan youth suffered prior abuse
medical.summary: Nearly every incarcerated male youth in a new University of Michigan study had experienced some form of physical abuse.

medical.title: A missing piece in the cell death and inflammation signaling pathway puzzle has been revealed
medical.summary: An international research team has discovered a previously unknown mechanism that plays a key role in the signaling pathways involved in programmed cell death. The team identified the protein HERC4 as an essential component of both TNF-induced necroptosis and apoptosis pathways—two processes that play a crucial role in maintaining cellular balance and triggering inflammatory responses.

medical.title: Experimental mRNA therapy dramatically extends treatment window for acetaminophen overdose in preclinical models
medical.summary: When a patient arrives at the hospital with an acetaminophen overdose, it's often a race against the clock. The only FDA-approved antidote for overdose-related liver injury, N‑acetylcysteine, must be administered within hours to be effective.

medical.title: Airway lining fights infection by physically removing infected cells, experiments show
medical.summary: The epithelium, a layer of cells that forms a protective barrier between the body and the outside world, was the first organized tissue to evolve. Epithelial cells lining our airways are mainly seen as a structural barrier, but cell biologist Jody Rosenblatt, who runs a lab at the Crick and King's College London, believes their evolutionary history suggests they play a much more active role in infections.

medical.title: How much do Americans spend on GLP-1 medications? Medical students measure drug affordability
medical.summary: The number of people using GLP-1 treatments like Ozempic and Wegovy for weight loss or chronic conditions has increased rapidly, with more than 1 in 10 U.S. adults currently taking such medications. A new study led by medical students at Virginia Commonwealth University has shed light on how this rise in GLP-1 drug use is affecting Americans' wallets.

medical.title: Death is certain but few of us are really prepared
medical.summary: Death may well come for us all, but new research has found that few Australians are prepared for it or know how to help family members at the end of their lives.

medical.title: Noninvasive nerve stimulation shows potential for treating uncontrolled high blood pressure
medical.summary: A noninvasive technique that stimulates nerves through the ear has been shown to be safe, well tolerated and easy for patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure to use at home, according to a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London.

medical.title: Exploring how brain aging influences language issues after stroke
medical.summary: After a stroke, even areas of the brain not directly affected by the injury can show signs of accelerated aging. Stroke can also lead to aphasia, a language disorder that varies widely in severity and treatment outlook. In a new study in JNeurosci, Nicholas Riccardi, Leonardo Bonilha and colleagues at the University of South Carolina Floyd School of Medicine examined how aging in uninjured areas of the brain relates to aphasia severity and recovery after treatment.

medical.title: Forest landscapes and birdsong soundscapes have independent physical health benefits
medical.summary: A new study finds that exposure to birdsong soundscapes or forest landscapes reduces physiological stress. These findings of physical health effects complement previous research showing mental health benefits associated with birdwatching and could be useful for urban planners with limited green space options.

medical.title: New study helps explain how endometriosis causes pain
medical.summary: One of the puzzling aspects of endometriosis—a gynecologic condition in which tissue similar to that lining the uterus grows outside of it—is that the extent of the disease doesn't determine the severity of its symptoms. New Yale research may help explain why some patients with a small number of growths experience debilitating pain, while others with more widespread disease have no symptoms.

medical.title: Are there toxic chemicals in your grocery store receipt?
medical.summary: "Would you like your receipt?"

medical.title: Life after… a diagnosis for panic disorder
medical.summary: Molly Lambert went viral discussing OCD, helping others recognise frightening experiences they’d been too scared to share The post Life after… a diagnosis for panic disorder appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Scientists discover cells that cheat death and rebuild damaged tissue
medical.summary: Scientists discovered a population of cells that can start the process of programmed cell death, survive it, and then help rapidly rebuild damaged tissue. Their descendants become far more resistant to future damage, revealing a mechanism that could improve healing but may also help cancers return after treatment.

medical.title: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice
medical.summary: Scientists found that declining levels of the brain protein Menin may help drive aging, with lower levels in mice linked to inflammation, cognitive decline, weaker bones, and thinner skin. Restoring Menin reversed several age-related changes, while the amino acid D-serine improved cognition, hinting at a potentially intriguing new target for healthy aging.

medical.title: Ozempic can change your body. Can it change your life?
medical.summary: Ozempic and other GLP-1 medications can improve blood sugar, weight, and cardiovascular health, but researchers found little evidence that they also improve mental health, employment, marriage, or overall well-being. The findings suggest the drugs’ broader life effects may be subtler than their dramatic physical health benefits.

science.title: Study across 40 countries: Political activism linked to representation
science.summary: Not happy with the election result? Don't worry. Election Day is not the only opportunity to influence politics.

science.title: How Bolsonaro's statements destroyed the rainforest
science.summary: Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro contributed to deforestation through statements opposing forest conservation, according to an international study led by the University of Bonn. The study found that destruction of the Amazon rainforest accelerated when Bolsonaro and his ministers posted messages opposing forest conservation on Twitter. Brazil's environmental authorities were greatly weakened during Bolsonaro's presidency, but the analysis suggests that even a perceived low risk of punishment was a driver of deforestation. The researchers estimate that the statements contributed to the destruction of up to 1,700 square kilometers (660 square miles) of forest—almost double the area of Berlin. The results were published in The Journal of Politics.

science.title: Dopamine-based nanotubes combine heat, electrical stimulation and antioxidant release for first time
science.summary: The research group at the Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia in Pontedera (Pisa), led by Gianni Ciofani, has developed new organic nanoparticles that combine multiple therapeutic functions in a single material for the first time.

science.title: Party leaders widening Washington's political chasm
science.summary: Most of the polarization currently roiling Congress comes from political parties rather than individual politicians, a study co-authored by University of Miami Business School associate professor Chad Kendall finds.

science.title: Plasma treatment helps reveal how molecular coatings dope silicon
science.summary: Controlling dopant concentration near the silicon surface is increasingly important for ultrashallow junctions and nanoscale devices. Mixed monolayer doping (MMLD) offers a surface-chemistry-based approach in which dopant-containing molecules are mixed with nondopant molecules to tune the amount of dopant available at the silicon surface before thermal diffusion.

science.title: Two-color glowing molecule could make wind tunnel tests more accurate
science.summary: Most sensors can measure only one thing at a time, like a thermometer for temperature or a pressure gauge for pressure. Measuring two properties accurately from the same surface at the same moment usually means using two separate instruments—adding cost and complexity to the process.

science.title: Espionage boosted East Germany's economic output by 7.4%
science.summary: East Germany's espionage activities in the West boosted the country's economic output by 7.4%. Value added in manufacturing alone increased by 22.3% through industrial espionage, equivalent to 20.2 billion East German marks or approximately 4.1 billion euros at 2020 prices.

science.title: Hydrogen's distant glow opens new way to investigate dark energy
science.summary: The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) has shown for the first time that it can detect the faint glow of hydrogen gas from deep in the universe's past using only its own data.

science.title: October’s Night Sky Notes: Spooky Stargazing
science.summary: The Ghoul Located within the constellation Perseus lies a star called Algol, also known as ‘Demon Star’ or ‘The Ghoul’. You can spot this star during the autumn months, along with Cassiopeia and Andromeda in the northeastern sky, beginning after 9 PM. In Greek mythology, this star represents the ‘blinking eye’ of the gorgon Medusa. […]

science.title: AI news coverage reveals hierarchy of innovators, regulators and overlooked regions
science.summary: Analyzing more than 43,000 English-language newspaper articles, a new study reveals a highly stratified narrative about AI in which the news media allocate authority unequally, reinforcing the technology's prominent role in contemporary life.

science.title: Assembly pathway reveals how bacteria build protein coils that extend in acid
science.summary: The assembly pathway behind refractile-body proteins may have finally been resolved, researchers from Science Tokyo report. Using genetic engineering and several techniques for analyzing protein structure, they investigated how four proteins work together to produce the correct architecture of these complex, pH-responsive protein machines, from the nanoscale to the microscale. The findings could help establish new frameworks for engineering dynamic protein systems as biotechnological tools.

science.title: Avian odysseys: Tracking raptor migrations from Europe to Africa
science.summary: At the southwest tip of Sweden, the Falsterbo Peninsula stretches into the Baltic Sea, creating a natural bottleneck for hundreds of millions of birds traveling south for the winter each year. Falsterbo is particularly known for raptor migration. One autumn morning, I stood with a group of others by the lighthouse, watching birds gather to cross the open sea—a sight to take your breath away.

science.title: European rivers are improving, but not fast enough to meet 2030 goals
science.summary: The quality of European rivers has improved in recent years, but not at the pace required to meet the environmental targets set for 2030. This is one of the main conclusions of a study led by researchers María Pachés Giner and Remedios Martínez from the Institute of Water and Environmental Engineering at the Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV), published in Environmental Science and Pollution Research.

environment.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
environment.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. environment.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

environment.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
environment.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

environment.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
environment.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

environment.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
environment.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

environment.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
environment.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

environment.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
environment.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

environment.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
environment.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

environment.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
environment.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: How Bolsonaro's statements destroyed the rainforest
mix_items.summary: Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro contributed to deforestation through statements opposing forest conservation, according to an international study led by the University of Bonn. The study found that destruction of the Amazon rainforest accelerated when Bolsonaro and his ministers posted messages opposing forest conservation on Twitter. Brazil's environmental authorities were greatly weakened during Bolsonaro's presidency, but the analysis suggests that even a perceived low risk of punishment was a driver of deforestation. The researchers estimate that the statements contributed to the destruction of up to 1,700 square kilometers (660 square miles) of forest—almost double the area of Berlin. The results were published in The Journal of Politics.

mix_items.title: Party leaders widening Washington's political chasm
mix_items.summary: Most of the polarization currently roiling Congress comes from political parties rather than individual politicians, a study co-authored by University of Miami Business School associate professor Chad Kendall finds.

mix_items.title: Plasma treatment helps reveal how molecular coatings dope silicon
mix_items.summary: Controlling dopant concentration near the silicon surface is increasingly important for ultrashallow junctions and nanoscale devices. Mixed monolayer doping (MMLD) offers a surface-chemistry-based approach in which dopant-containing molecules are mixed with nondopant molecules to tune the amount of dopant available at the silicon surface before thermal diffusion.

mix_items.title: Two-color glowing molecule could make wind tunnel tests more accurate
mix_items.summary: Most sensors can measure only one thing at a time, like a thermometer for temperature or a pressure gauge for pressure. Measuring two properties accurately from the same surface at the same moment usually means using two separate instruments—adding cost and complexity to the process.

mix_items.title: Espionage boosted East Germany's economic output by 7.4%
mix_items.summary: East Germany's espionage activities in the West boosted the country's economic output by 7.4%. Value added in manufacturing alone increased by 22.3% through industrial espionage, equivalent to 20.2 billion East German marks or approximately 4.1 billion euros at 2020 prices.

mix_items.title: Hydrogen's distant glow opens new way to investigate dark energy
mix_items.summary: The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) has shown for the first time that it can detect the faint glow of hydrogen gas from deep in the universe's past using only its own data.

mix_items.title: October’s Night Sky Notes: Spooky Stargazing
mix_items.summary: The Ghoul Located within the constellation Perseus lies a star called Algol, also known as ‘Demon Star’ or ‘The Ghoul’. You can spot this star during the autumn months, along with Cassiopeia and Andromeda in the northeastern sky, beginning after 9 PM. In Greek mythology, this star represents the ‘blinking eye’ of the gorgon Medusa. […]

mix_items.title: AI news coverage reveals hierarchy of innovators, regulators and overlooked regions
mix_items.summary: Analyzing more than 43,000 English-language newspaper articles, a new study reveals a highly stratified narrative about AI in which the news media allocate authority unequally, reinforcing the technology's prominent role in contemporary life.

mix_items.title: Assembly pathway reveals how bacteria build protein coils that extend in acid
mix_items.summary: The assembly pathway behind refractile-body proteins may have finally been resolved, researchers from Science Tokyo report. Using genetic engineering and several techniques for analyzing protein structure, they investigated how four proteins work together to produce the correct architecture of these complex, pH-responsive protein machines, from the nanoscale to the microscale. The findings could help establish new frameworks for engineering dynamic protein systems as biotechnological tools.

mix_items.title: Avian odysseys: Tracking raptor migrations from Europe to Africa
mix_items.summary: At the southwest tip of Sweden, the Falsterbo Peninsula stretches into the Baltic Sea, creating a natural bottleneck for hundreds of millions of birds traveling south for the winter each year. Falsterbo is particularly known for raptor migration. One autumn morning, I stood with a group of others by the lighthouse, watching birds gather to cross the open sea—a sight to take your breath away.

mix_items.title: European rivers are improving, but not fast enough to meet 2030 goals
mix_items.summary: The quality of European rivers has improved in recent years, but not at the pace required to meet the environmental targets set for 2030. This is one of the main conclusions of a study led by researchers María Pachés Giner and Remedios Martínez from the Institute of Water and Environmental Engineering at the Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV), published in Environmental Science and Pollution Research.

mix_items.title: Fluctuations in blood pressure over time linked to death and strokes, analysis of UK data finds
mix_items.summary: Greater variation in blood pressure between research visits was associated with a higher risk of death in a study of more than 57,000 UK Biobank participants. Variation in some blood pressure measures was also associated with stroke. The findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2.

mix_items.title: Regulator-mandated study finds no link between semaglutide use and pancreatic cancer
mix_items.summary: New research presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2, found no link between semaglutide use and pancreatic cancer in nationwide registry data from Denmark, Sweden and Norway. The regulator-mandated post-authorization study was presented by Anton Pottegård, a professor at the University of Southern Denmark in Odense, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Just 20 seconds of speech could help detect type 2 diabetes using AI-based tool
mix_items.summary: Signs of type 2 diabetes can be detected in just a few seconds from the way someone talks, according to research being presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2.

mix_items.title: How moving neighborhood can alter risk of type 2 diabetes
mix_items.summary: Where someone lives strongly influences their risk of developing type 2 diabetes, new research from Canada suggests. The research was presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy, Sept. 28–Oct. 2.

mix_items.title: Supervised physical therapy improves short-term knee pain and function after ACL surgery in young adults
mix_items.summary: A randomized clinical trial found that supervised physical therapy after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) surgery yielded greater improvements in pain, function and muscle strength than a self-directed exercise program, at least in the short term. The findings can inform care for people with ongoing knee symptoms after ACL surgery. The study is published in Annals of Internal Medicine.

mix_items.title: Study revisits measures of breastfeeding success—and the consequences for parents
mix_items.summary: Within breastfeeding research, there's a widely recognized need to move beyond using only the duration of breastfeeding as the measure of "successful breastfeeding" and to integrate person-centered outcomes.

mix_items.title: Bedside blood test can deliver results in under 10 minutes to guide urgent stroke care
mix_items.summary: Minutes count when a patient with a stroke arrives at a hospital emergency room. Doctors stand ready to treat the patient, but whether medication can dissolve the blood clot depends on what the patient is already taking. Even if a blood sample is rushed to the laboratory, results can take up to an hour to arrive.

mix_items.title: Lower dietary diversity in the first year linked to atopic dermatitis
mix_items.summary: Lower dietary diversity during the first year of life is associated with an increased risk of atopic dermatitis (AD) later in life, according to a study published online Sept. 20 in Pediatric Allergy and Immunology.

mix_items.title: Metabolic activity of gut bacteria can either promote or inhibit function of CAR T cells in cancer therapy
mix_items.summary: Immunotherapies, especially CAR T-cell therapy, have fundamentally changed cancer treatment in recent years, particularly for certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma. Yet not all tumors respond equally well, and the reasons for this remain incompletely understood. A new multicenter study by the Leibniz Institute for Immunotherapy collaboration group, Innate Immune Sensing in Cancer and Transplantation, now shows that it is not only the composition of the gut microbiota that determines the success of CAR T-cell therapy, but above all its metabolic products.

mix_items.title: Abuse and disability trap: 90% of incarcerated Michigan youth suffered prior abuse
mix_items.summary: Nearly every incarcerated male youth in a new University of Michigan study had experienced some form of physical abuse.

mix_items.title: A missing piece in the cell death and inflammation signaling pathway puzzle has been revealed
mix_items.summary: An international research team has discovered a previously unknown mechanism that plays a key role in the signaling pathways involved in programmed cell death. The team identified the protein HERC4 as an essential component of both TNF-induced necroptosis and apoptosis pathways—two processes that play a crucial role in maintaining cellular balance and triggering inflammatory responses.

mix_items.title: Experimental mRNA therapy dramatically extends treatment window for acetaminophen overdose in preclinical models
mix_items.summary: When a patient arrives at the hospital with an acetaminophen overdose, it's often a race against the clock. The only FDA-approved antidote for overdose-related liver injury, N‑acetylcysteine, must be administered within hours to be effective.

mix_items.title: Airway lining fights infection by physically removing infected cells, experiments show
mix_items.summary: The epithelium, a layer of cells that forms a protective barrier between the body and the outside world, was the first organized tissue to evolve. Epithelial cells lining our airways are mainly seen as a structural barrier, but cell biologist Jody Rosenblatt, who runs a lab at the Crick and King's College London, believes their evolutionary history suggests they play a much more active role in infections.

mix_items.title: How much do Americans spend on GLP-1 medications? Medical students measure drug affordability
mix_items.summary: The number of people using GLP-1 treatments like Ozempic and Wegovy for weight loss or chronic conditions has increased rapidly, with more than 1 in 10 U.S. adults currently taking such medications. A new study led by medical students at Virginia Commonwealth University has shed light on how this rise in GLP-1 drug use is affecting Americans' wallets.

mix_items.title: Death is certain but few of us are really prepared
mix_items.summary: Death may well come for us all, but new research has found that few Australians are prepared for it or know how to help family members at the end of their lives.

mix_items.title: Noninvasive nerve stimulation shows potential for treating uncontrolled high blood pressure
mix_items.summary: A noninvasive technique that stimulates nerves through the ear has been shown to be safe, well tolerated and easy for patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure to use at home, according to a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London.

mix_items.title: Exploring how brain aging influences language issues after stroke
mix_items.summary: After a stroke, even areas of the brain not directly affected by the injury can show signs of accelerated aging. Stroke can also lead to aphasia, a language disorder that varies widely in severity and treatment outlook. In a new study in JNeurosci, Nicholas Riccardi, Leonardo Bonilha and colleagues at the University of South Carolina Floyd School of Medicine examined how aging in uninjured areas of the brain relates to aphasia severity and recovery after treatment.

mix_items.title: Forest landscapes and birdsong soundscapes have independent physical health benefits
mix_items.summary: A new study finds that exposure to birdsong soundscapes or forest landscapes reduces physiological stress. These findings of physical health effects complement previous research showing mental health benefits associated with birdwatching and could be useful for urban planners with limited green space options.

mix_items.title: New study helps explain how endometriosis causes pain
mix_items.summary: One of the puzzling aspects of endometriosis—a gynecologic condition in which tissue similar to that lining the uterus grows outside of it—is that the extent of the disease doesn't determine the severity of its symptoms. New Yale research may help explain why some patients with a small number of growths experience debilitating pain, while others with more widespread disease have no symptoms.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover cells that cheat death and rebuild damaged tissue
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered a population of cells that can start the process of programmed cell death, survive it, and then help rapidly rebuild damaged tissue. Their descendants become far more resistant to future damage, revealing a mechanism that could improve healing but may also help cancers return after treatment.

mix_items.title: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice
mix_items.summary: Scientists found that declining levels of the brain protein Menin may help drive aging, with lower levels in mice linked to inflammation, cognitive decline, weaker bones, and thinner skin. Restoring Menin reversed several age-related changes, while the amino acid D-serine improved cognition, hinting at a potentially intriguing new target for healthy aging.

mix_items.title: Ozempic can change your body. Can it change your life?
mix_items.summary: Ozempic and other GLP-1 medications can improve blood sugar, weight, and cardiovascular health, but researchers found little evidence that they also improve mental health, employment, marriage, or overall well-being. The findings suggest the drugs’ broader life effects may be subtler than their dramatic physical health benefits.

mix_items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
mix_items.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

mix_items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
mix_items.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.
